chunks: It is narrated from Ya'qub ibn Shu'ayb, who said:

I asked Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام. I said: I give a man the price, twenty dinars, and say to him: If your fruit reaches some value, then it is mine for that price; if I am satisfied, I take it, and if I dislike it, I leave it.
So he said: "Can you not give it to him without stipulating anything?"
I said: May I be your ransom! And what if he does not specify anything, while Allah knows that to be his intention?
He said: "It is not valid if that is his intention."

key_terms.الثَّمَنَ: the purchase price paid in the transaction
key_terms.تَشْتَرِطَ: to stipulate a condition in the agreement
key_terms.ثَمَرَتُكَ: your fruit, meaning the produce being discussed for sale
key_terms.عِشْرِينَ دِينَارًا: twenty dinars as the stated amount of payment
key_terms.لَا يَصْلُحُ: it is not valid or sound in legal effect
key_terms.نِيَّتِهِ: his intention, including the concealed purpose behind the deal

ai.seo_question: Is a sale valid if a hidden condition is intended but not stated openly?
ai.summary: This hadith addresses a sale arrangement involving advance payment for fruit with an unstated or conditional understanding that the buyer may later accept or decline. Imam al-Sadiq عليه السلام rejects both explicit stipulation and concealed intention of such a condition, indicating the legal invalidity of a transaction built on an undisclosed condition.
